National Grid Failure?

By: Julian Sun | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
What plans have been put in place to mitigate against the nightmare scenario of a National Grid Failure

Unique Selling Point:
We speak to the people in charge of disaster management to give you the information you need to know should the unthinkable happen and the National Grid fail

Summary:
As SA prepares for a long, dark winter, Stage 8 loadshedding is the best-case scenario we can hope for. Loadshedding is implemented to prevent a catastrophic national grid failure. While many experts say this won’t happen, the probability of this nightmare scenario becomes ever greater as our failing national grid buckles.

One only needs to look at what happened in Venezuela when its grid collapsed in 2019 due to poor maintenance. It’s estimated that it could take a minimum of 6-14 days to restart the grid, with terrifying consequences:

What plans have been put in place should the national grid fail? We speak to Disaster Management Planners from various levels of government to find out how we'd cope should this nightmare scenario come to pass.

Colin Deiner
Isabel Fick
Mark Swilling

Script:


V/O: South Africa is in the grip of the worst energy crisis in its history.

Sound Up: Of course, Eskom went from stage 3 and 4 to stage 6, this is in a matter of hours

Sound up: It’s going to be a cold dark night for many South Africans

Our aging, crumbling national grid is no longer fit for purpose with daily power cuts of up to 12 hours.

As the icy grip of winter descends over the country, will the extra demand for power push an already-buckling grid to the brink?

Sound Up: We are staring down the barrel of stage 8 blackouts

Sound Up So as load-shedding persists daily, fears of a complete national blackout continue to circulate
rr
JULIUS MALEMA: There’s going to be darkness, we’re almost at the point of grid collapse!

OPENING LINK: But are we? It’s a nightmare scenario too ghastly to contemplate, the failure of the grid leading to a national blackout. It would take days to weeks to restart and the results would be catastrophic.
V/O: Here’s how it might play out:
A sudden, unexpected event destabilizes the grid. Within a matter of milliseconds, automatic failsafes trigger causing every power station to automatically shut down.
With no electricity, traffic lights go down causing road chaos. Emergency Services in major cities scramble into action …
Fire Station sequence
V/O: After a few hours, reserve batteries begin to run dry. ATMS stop functioning, as-do fuel pumps
Telecommunications is the next to fail, we can no longer make calls or use the internet
Within 24 hours, food begins to spoil, as supermarkets run out of goods

2 days in, water purification plants fail and the taps run dry

After 3 days, there is a shift to a cash-based economy, riots break out all around the country.
V/O: But to understand how the grid could collapse, one first needs to know how it works

It begins with 30 coal-fired power stations and 86 renewables operated by Eskom. These generate electricity which then travels across the country on the pylons that form the vast transmission network. This is then fed into homes and businesses in the final part of the network called the distribution system.

But what would cause it to fail?

Professor Mark Swilling is an energy expert at Stellenbosch University
Mark Swilling: [00:01:52] There's a certain frequency that has to be achieved on the grid for the electricity to be transmitted effectively. [00:02:36][44.5]
Mark Swilling: [00:09:53] If there is a simultaneous tripping of two or three power stations that could trigger a drop in the level in the frequency level on the grid, which in turn could trigger responses and all the other healthy generators who are now getting a signal, hey, the grid is no longer adequate to continue to supply and they start switching off. And then you have this domino effect
Isabel Fick: [00:05:53] In the end, you then have a total grid collapse, which then means that there is no power anywhere on the network.
LINK 2: The duty of operating and protecting the national grid lies with Eskom. If it were to collapse the responsibility of restarting it lies with the engineers working here.

V/O: That team is led by Isabel Fick, General Manager for the System Operator at Eskom.

Isabel: We have the best people in the world doing this. You can just imagine we are load shedding every single day, no one else is doing this.

V/O: In other words, Eskom has become a world leader in managing the grid through load-shedding



V/O: Grid collapse is an extremely rare event but it does happen. Globally there have been a number of blackouts over the past few years, the most serious in Venezuela in 2019
Venezuela montage
V/O: With eerie echoes of South Africa’s energy crisis, mismanagement and poor maintenance of their national grid caused it to fail, leaving 30 million people without power for a week.
In February 2021, an intense winter storm in Texas took down its power grid leaving over 4 million without heat or water for 4 days. 150 people lost their lives.
V/O: Closer to home, our neighbours Botswana suffered a country-wide blackout in May but thanks to help from Eskom, were able to restart their grid in a few hours
Mark Swilling: [00:11:23] Botswana and South Africa are in the southern African power pool, which is an interconnected grid system. But South Africa is by far the biggest generator of electricity in that system. So we can supply a very small, uh, user of electricity like Botswana when they are in a crisis. but not the reverse.
V/O: If our grid were to collapse, we’re on our own. That’s why it’s crucial to keep it stable. One of Eskom's main tools to do this is something all South Africans hate: Load-shedding
Erin: [00:08:16] As a layperson, I think we're getting higher and higher levels of load-shedding. We must be closer and closer to grid collapse. Am I right?
Mark Swilling: [00:08:26] No, not. Not really. Loadshedding is actually a mechanism to prevent the collapse of the grid. So, in essence, the worse that load-shedding is, the better it is for the grid. It's strange, but that's not how South Africans think.
Isabel Fick: [00:11:32] You are no closer to a national blackout when you're in stage one than you are on stage eight and I think we need to make that clear.
Erin: [00:12:53] There's no causal link now between higher load-shedding levels and the probability of a blackout.
Isabel Fick: [00:13:00] No blackout is a sudden unexpected event that happens suddenly and can be foreseen.
V/O: As the saying goes, Fail to plan, plan to fail and some organizations are making contingencies.
The Reserve Bank has been working on a plan to ensure that the financial sector continues to function during a blackout.
We reached out for an interview but our request was turned down
The National Disaster Management Centre, also chose not to comment
The only organization willing to go on record was the Western Cape Provincial Government. Colin Deiner is the head of disaster management in the province.
Colin Deiner: [00:02:15] We already started around 2014. We had a meeting at the National Disaster Management Centre and we had the Eskom risk people. At that meeting. They indicated to us that it's prudent for us to plan for a national blackout. [00:02:28][13.1]
Colin Deiner: [00:04:38] Our primary objective to protect the province in the event of an incident like this and to protect lives. [00:04:50][11.6]
Colin Deiner: [00:05:20] So I think what's really important is that a grid collapse is an extremely unlikely scenario. [00:05:26][6.1]
Colin Deiner: [00:05:58] But because of of the fact that it's a risk, you know, within our system, we do plan for it as we would plan for, you know, a nuclear incident, as we would plan for everything else. [00:06:09][10.7]
Erin: [00:18:42] Let's say that day comes, that dread day comes and we're hit with a national blackout. How would that play out?
Colin Deiner: [00:19:45] We have structures in place, Our provincial government will come to the disaster centre. They will be the provincial cabinet with all the senior people and they will then be briefed by ourselves, by Eskom as to what to expect [00:20:14][28.5]
Colin Deiner: [00:19:07] our biggest challenge on that on the day, if we can look at it in that in that context, is that there would possibly be no warning [00:19:19][11.8]
Colin Deiner: The other thing is that it impacts the entire community. The immensity of planning for this and having to meet with so many sectors and to ensure that the planning is in place is really where the challenge lies
V/O: With the country shrouded in perpetual darkness, the race would be on to restore power - a process that could take days, if not weeks.
Isabel Fick: [00:40:04] Our own planning tells us it's about between six days and 14 days to restore the national grid.
Isabel Fick: [00:42:19] t will definitely be a staggered approach. you have to do it in a very stable and controlled manner. You don't want to have a secondary collapse.
Colin Deiner: [00:41:24] We've got to remember that we're going to have to recover from this. So it won't be two weeks and everything will be fine. Everything that took a hit and got damaged over that period is going to have to be stabilised. So it's not just the question of, you know, the lights are going to come on and everything will be fine again. [00:42:01][36.9]
CLOSING LINK: With so much anxiety around the state of the national grid, it’s easy to give in to fears it might soon collapse.

V/O: But Ironically higher levels of load-shedding should actually reassure us that the grid remains safe, yet social media is still abuzz with fears of a blackout
Erin: [00:45:15] So I'm hearing you give us a lot of reassurance, which is very much in contrast with the kind of messaging happening in WhatsApp groups and on online forums, social media,
Isabel Fick: [00:45:42] Well, first of all, yes, I am very much aware, and I think I'm the first one to get all of them. I think it's a very irresponsible tool to prompt panic amongst our citizens. The probability is extremely small
Isabel Fick: [00:46:35] You don't need to panic. There is no reason to to suspect that this is going to happen any time soon. It hasn't happened in 100 years. So for us to to now go into a frenzy and think it's going to happen now just simply doesn't make any sense
President Ramaphosa: The risk of a national blackout remains extremely low.

V/O: Cold comfort but, provided the president is right, comfort nonetheless.
